87:14.title: Purification, Prayer, and the Choice of Worlds
87:14.in_short: True success belongs to whoever purifies himself, remembers his Lord, and prays. Yet people choose this fleeting world over the Hereafter, though the Hereafter is better and lasts forever. This same teaching, the commentators note, was already written in the earlier scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa.

claims.text: The general meaning of 'whoever purifies himself' (tazakkā) is one who cleanses himself from disbelief, sin, and bad character, and follows what Allah revealed.

sources.original_excerpt: من تطهَّر من الكفر ومعاصي الله
طهر نفسه ونقاها من الشرك والظلم ومساوئ الأخلاق

claims.text: Some early exegetes narrow the meaning to giving zakat al-fitr specifically, citing the practice of 'Umar b. 'Abdul-'Aziz who recited this verse when commanding people to give it, and reports from Ibn Sirin, Abu al-'Aliya and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

report.graded_by: not specified in provided sources

claims.text: Al-Sa'di holds that readings tying the verse to zakat al-fitr or the eid prayer are included within the word's scope but are not its sole or complete meaning; the verse's meaning is broader.

sources.original_excerpt: فإنه وإن كان داخلًا في اللفظ وبعض جزئياته، فليس هو المعنى وحده

claims.text: Others read tazakkā as giving zakat on one's wealth generally, not the fitr charity specifically.
Others read tazakkā as testifying 'there is no god but Allah', purifying oneself from association of partners with Him (shirk).

report.graded_by: not specified

claims.text: A historical report ties the verse to 'Uthman b. 'Affan, who bought a date-palm from a hypocrite so an Ansari neighbour would no longer be harmed by his dispute over its fruit; another report links it to Abu Bakr.

report.graded_by: al-Qurtubi (no grading given)

claims.text: Israr Ahmad reads tazakkā as the purification of the soul itself, connecting it to Surah al-Tin's account of man created in the best form then cast down to the lowest; the goal of worldly life is to raise the soul back up by weakening bodily desire and feeding the soul, a discipline modelled in the daily rhythm of Ramadan (fasting by day, night prayer with Qur'an by night).

sources.original_excerpt: تَزَکّٰیسے مراد یہاں روح کی پاکیزگی ہے

claims.text: Some questioned linking the verse to zakat al-fitr or the eid prayer, since the surah is Meccan and neither institution existed in Mecca; al-Baghawi answers that revelation can precede the ruling it points to, as with other verses (e.g. the freedom of Mecca announced before the Conquest); al-Qurtubi notes the majority view that the surah is Meccan and cites al-Qushayri's answer that praise here may extend to future compliance.

'Remembered the name of his Lord' means he affirmed God's oneness; al-Tabari concludes the correct view combines this with invoking and calling upon Him, since dhikr (remembrance) is not restricted to one form.

sources.original_excerpt: وحَّد الله فوحَّده، ودعاه ورغب إليه

claims.text: 'Then prayed' (fa ṣallā) is understood to cover the five daily prayers, both obligatory and supererogatory.

An alternative, narrower reading ties both dhikr and prayer specifically to the 'Id: the takbirs of the festival and the 'Id prayer, following the practice of giving charity (zakat al-fitr) before it, as reported of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar.

report.graded_by: not specified

claims.text: Another reading takes 'prayed' (ṣallā) here to mean supplication (du'a) rather than the ritual prayer.

Al-Qurtubi notes the verse is used as evidence that the opening takbir (takbirat al-iḥrām) is a distinct act from the prayer itself, since it is joined to it by 'and' (fa), and cites the resulting dispute among jurists over whether the opening may be pronounced with any name of Allah.

Al-Qurtubi records further glosses on 'remembered the name of his Lord': that it means remembering one's return and standing before God, which moves one to worship; or remembering God inwardly during the prayer so that fear and hope shape one's devotion; or opening every recitation with the Basmalah, with dhikr and prayer named in either order without difference of meaning.

Al-Sa'di reads the verse as saying that being characterised by remembrance colours the heart, and this necessarily produces action pleasing to God, especially prayer, which he calls 'the scale of faith' (mīzān al-īmān).

sources.original_excerpt: الصلاة، التي هي ميزان الإيمان

claims.text: Israr Ahmad takes the Friday congregation as the practical picture of this verse: remembrance in the sermon (khutbah) followed by prayer, drawing on hadith describing the Prophet's ﷺ two short khutbahs and a hadith about angels recording the order of early arrivals at the Friday prayer.

report.graded_by: Israr Ahmad (hadiths cited without grading)

claims.text: Sayyid Qutb reads remembrance and prayer together as instilling awe of God in the heart, producing success in this world (a heart alive and connected to God, tasting sweetness in remembrance) and in the Hereafter (safety from the great Fire and lasting bliss in the Gardens).
The general meaning of the verse is that people prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter.

The reciters differ on this word: the majority read tu'thirūn (you prefer, addressing people directly), while Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read yu'thirūn (they prefer), referring back to 'the most wretched' (al-ashqā) mentioned earlier in the surah.
The reading of Ubayy b. Ka'b, 'bal antum tu'thirūn' (Rather, you prefer), is cited as supporting evidence for the majority's second-person reading.

Ibn Mas'ud, on reaching this verse, paused and told his companions: 'We have preferred this world over the Hereafter,' because the world's pleasures, women, food and drink, are presented to us now, while the Hereafter is hidden from view.

report.graded_by: not specified in provided sources

claims.text: Al-Tantawi records that many scholars take the address here as directed at the disbelievers specifically, a shift of address (iltifāt) supported by Abu 'Amr's third-person reading, though the address to 'people' in general also includes believers who often occupy themselves with worldly benefit at the expense of the Hereafter.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari told Anas that what holds people back is not desire itself but that the world is 'hastened' and immediately present while the Hereafter is hidden from sight; had people seen it clearly, they would not have swerved from it.

report.graded_by: not specified

claims.text: Sayyid Qutb calls love of this world the root of every calamity, the reason man turns from admonition, since the Hereafter demands giving it priority; he notes that the very word 'dunya' comes from a root meaning 'near' or 'base', signalling its nearness and quick passing against the Hereafter's excellence and permanence.

original_terms.gloss: this-worldly life, from a root meaning 'near' or 'base'

claims.text: Israr Ahmad states that a person's success or failure in the Hereafter depends entirely on his priorities; the underlying disease is that worldly gain and loss are immediately visible ('cash'), while the comfort or pain of the Hereafter is unseen, a point he links to the Qur'an's warning about devouring orphans' wealth (Q4:10) and to the parallel statement in Surah al-Qiyamah about loving 'the hastening one' and leaving the Hereafter.
The general meaning is that the Hereafter is better in quality and more lasting than this transient world.
A hadith is cited comparing this world to the Hereafter as a finger dipped into the sea, showing how little the world contains next to what remains behind.

report.graded_by: al-Qurtubi and Zakariya, citing Sahih Muslim

claims.text: Malik b. Dinar is quoted saying that even if this world were gold that perishes and the Hereafter clay that lasts, the lasting clay would still deserve preference, how much more since the Hereafter is in fact gold that lasts and this world clay that perishes.

Mufti Muhammad Shafi' illustrates the choice with two houses: a furnished mansion available only briefly, or a modest house owned permanently; a wise person prefers permanence, so the Hereafter, even were it hypothetically inferior, deserves preference for enduring forever, and in fact it is also superior.

Ibn Kathir cites a hadith, transmitted alone by Imam Ahmad from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever loves his worldly life will harm his Hereafter, and whoever loves his Hereafter will harm his worldly life; so prefer what remains over what perishes.'

report.graded_by: Ibn Kathir (notes Ahmad alone transmitted it)

claims.text: Al-Sa'di states that loving this world and preferring it over the Hereafter is 'the root of every sin' (ra's kull khaṭī'ah).

sources.original_excerpt: فحب الدنيا وإيثارها على الآخرة رأس كل خطيئة

claims.text: Exegetes differ on what 'this' (hādhā) refers to: the verses of this surah generally ('Ikrimah); the story/content of this surah (Abu al-'Aliya); what is related in this surah (Qatada); or specifically the statement that the Hereafter is better and more lasting (Qatada, Ibn Zayd). Al-Tabari prefers that it points back to the preceding four verses as a whole, and Ibn Kathir endorses this as 'good and strong'.

Al-Qurtubi also records that al-Kalbi held 'this' spans from 'qad aflaḥa' to the end of the surah, appealing to the hadith of Abu Dharr, while al-Dahhak read it as saying the Qur'an itself is present in the earlier scriptures.

The 'earlier scriptures' are identified as the scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa عليهما السلام, meaning these truths, self-purification, prayer, and the superiority of the Hereafter, were already taught in earlier revelation.

Ibn Kathir cross-references Surah al-Najm (53:36-42) as parallel material about the scriptures of Musa and Ibrahim, 'who fulfilled', covering that no soul bears another's burden and that man gets only what he has striven for.

Mufti Muhammad Shafi' transmits, through al-Ajurri from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, a report describing the contents of the scriptures of Ibrahim (a parable warning a tyrant king that kingship is not for hoarding wealth but so that the oppressed's prayer may reach God, and advice that a wise man divides his time between worship, self-reckoning, and livelihood) and of Musa (four sayings of wonder about people who believe in death yet live carefree, believe in decree yet grieve, witness the world's turns yet remain content with it, and believe in the Reckoning yet abandon deeds). Abu Dharr then asked whether anything of these had been revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, who replied yes, and recited verses 14-19 of this surah.

report.graded_by: Mufti Muhammad Shafi' (via al-Ajurri, no grading given)

claims.text: Sayyid Qutb reads the shared content across the scriptures of Ibrahim, Musa, and the Qur'an as showing that truth is one, the creed is one, and the source of religion is one; laws differ according to the needs of each era, but all converge from the one 'Most High Lord' who created, proportioned, decreed, and guided everything.

87:14.essay_html:
The passage names two marks of the successful person: purifying himself (tazakkā) and remembering his Lord's name before prayer. The commentators agree on the broad sense, cleansing oneself from disbelief, sin and bad character, following what has been revealed.1,2,3,4,5,7,9,11,12,13,14 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) reads it more inwardly still: the soul was created in its best form and then cast down, so life's task is to lift it back up, weakening bodily appetite while feeding the soul, a rhythm he sees modelled in the discipline of Ramadan.8

Several early reports narrow tazakkā to a specific act: giving zakat al-fitr, following the practice of 'Umar b. 'Abdul-'Azīz and reports about Ibn Sīrīn and Abū Sa'īd al-Khudrī.1,2,3,4,14 Others read it as zakat on wealth generally,1,3 and others as the declaration of God's oneness itself.1,2,3 Al-Sa'dī (d. 1957) holds these narrower readings sit inside the word without exhausting it.5 A question was raised about tying the verse to zakat al-fitr or the 'Id prayer at all, since the surah is Meccan and neither institution yet existed there; al-Baghawī (d. 1122) answers that revelation can precede the ruling it points toward, as happens elsewhere in the Qur'an.2,3 A historical report also ties the verse to 'Uthmān ibn 'Affān, who traded a date-palm to spare an Anṣārī neighbour harm from a hypocrite's dispute.3

'Remembered the name of his Lord, and prayed' is read most simply as declaring God's oneness and performing the five daily prayers.1,3,7,9,11 Some narrow both dhikr and prayer to the takbīrs and prayer of the 'Id, tied to giving charity beforehand, as reported of Ibn Mas'ūd and Ibn 'Umar.1,2,3 Others take 'prayed' here as supplication rather than ritual prayer.1,3 Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) notes the verse used as evidence that the opening takbīr is a separate act from the prayer itself, a point disputed among jurists as to whether the opening may be said with any name of God.3 He also records further glosses: remembering one's standing before God, remembering Him inwardly during the prayer so fear and hope shape one's devotion, or opening each recitation with the Basmalah.3 Al-Sa'dī reads the verse as saying that being marked by remembrance colours the heart and necessarily produces righteous action, above all prayer, which he calls 'the scale of faith' (mīzān al-īmān).5 Isrār Aḥmad sees the Friday congregation as the living picture of the verse, remembrance in the sermon followed by prayer.8 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads remembrance and prayer together as planting God's awe in the heart, bringing success in this life, a heart alive and connected to God, and in the next, safety from the Fire and lasting bliss in the Gardens.6

The next verse turns from the successful to the crowd: 'you prefer the life of this world.' The reciters differ over whether this addresses people directly (tu'thirūn) or speaks of them in the third person (yu'thirūn), pointing back to 'the most wretched' named earlier in the surah; most read the direct address, supported by Ubayy's recitation 'rather, you prefer.'1,2,3,9 Al-Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010) notes some scholars take this as a shift of address aimed specifically at the disbelievers, though the wider address also touches believers who often chase worldly gain at their Hereafter's expense.9 A well-known report has Ibn Mas'ūd pausing on this verse to tell his companions plainly: 'we have preferred this world', because its pleasures are put before us now while the Hereafter stays hidden from sight.1,2,3,7 Abū Mūsā al-Ash'arī made the same point to Anas: it is not desire alone but the world's nearness against the Hereafter's concealment that pulls people astray.3 Sayyid Quṭb adds that the very word dunyā, from a root meaning 'near' or 'base', names this pull: quick, close and passing, against the Hereafter's excellence and permanence.6 Isrār Aḥmad frames it as a matter of priorities, worldly gain and loss are 'cash', visible now, while the Hereafter's comfort and pain are unseen, a pattern he links to the Qur'an's warnings elsewhere about wealth wrongly consumed and the love of what hastens.8

'The Hereafter is better and more lasting' draws a stack of illustrations from the commentators. A hadith likens this world beside the Hereafter to a finger dipped in the sea, whatever it brings back is all this world holds by comparison.3,11 Mālik ibn Dīnār is quoted saying that even if the world were perishing gold and the Hereafter lasting clay, the lasting clay would still deserve preference, let alone when the Hereafter is in truth the gold that lasts.3 Muftī Muḥammad Shafī' (d. 1976) pictures two houses, a furnished mansion held briefly against a modest house owned forever, and asks which a sensible person would choose.7 Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) records a hadith, transmitted alone by Imam Aḥmad, urging that one 'prefer what remains over what perishes,' while noting its single chain of transmission.4 Al-Sa'dī states plainly that loving this world over the Hereafter is 'the root of every sin.'5

Finally, 'this is in the earlier scriptures.' The exegetes differ on what 'this' points to: the whole surah, its story, what it relates, or specifically the statement that the Hereafter is better and more lasting. Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) prefers that it spans the four verses just given, and Ibn Kathīr calls this preference 'good and strong.'1,2,3,4 Al-Qurṭubī also records al-Kalbī's view that it spans the whole surah, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk's reading that the Qur'an itself is present in the earlier books.3 These earlier scriptures are named as those of Ibrāhīm and Mūsā عليهما السلام.2,4,9,13,14 Ibn Kathīr links this to Sūrat al-Najm's mention of the same two scriptures.4 Muftī Muḥammad Shafī' transmits, through Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, sayings said to belong to those scriptures, on the tyrant king who forgets that rule exists to let the oppressed's prayer reach God, on dividing one's time between worship, self-reckoning and livelihood, and wonder-sayings about people who believe in death yet live carefree, or believe in the Reckoning yet abandon deeds; Abū Dharr reports the Prophet ﷺ then recited these very verses to him.7 Sayyid Quṭb draws the conclusion that truth is one and its source is one, even where laws differ across the ages according to need.6

Across these readings the commentators return to one line: the world is near and quickly gone, the Hereafter is better and remains, and this was no new word but one already written before.1,3,4,5,9

87:10.title: The Fearful and the Wretched
87:10.in_short: The reminder lands on the person who fears God, who takes heed and benefits; the most wretched person turns away from it and ends up in the Greatest Fire, in a state the Qur'an calls neither death nor life.

claims.text: "Whoever fears" (man yakhsha) means the one who fears Allah and His punishment, hopes for His reward, and knows he will meet Him; because he expects to answer for his deeds, he benefits from the reminder and holds back from wrongdoing.

sources.original_excerpt: من يخشى الله، ويخاف عقابه
من يخشى، الله عز وجل
خشية الله تعالى، وعلمه بأن سيجازيه على أعماله
سينتفع بتذكيرك ... من يخشى الله
سيتعظ الذي يخاف ربه

claims.text: A report holds that this verse came down concerning Ibn Umm Maktum.

sources.original_excerpt: نزلت في ابن أم مكتوم

report.graded_by: not assessed by al-Qurtubi

claims.text: al-Mawardi is cited as saying that admonition reaches the one who fears more forcefully than it reaches the one who merely hopes, even though the reminder may in fact concern both; this is why the verse ties itself to fear rather than hope.

sources.original_excerpt: تذكرة الخاشي أبلغ من تذكرة الراجي

claims.text: Another view, attributed to al-Qushayri, holds that the meaning is: make your reminding general to everyone, for even though only the fearful truly benefit, the one who reminds still earns the reward of having called.

sources.original_excerpt: عمم أنت التذكير والوعظ

claims.text: The world's own signs (a serviceable animal like the camel obedient to man, the sky, the earth serving human need without effort) remind the thoughtful person of God and the Hereafter. Those who draw remembrance from them earn God's lasting bounty; those who remain in heedlessness prove they deserve to be deprived of it forever.
"He avoids it" (yatajannabuha) means the wretched one avoids the reminder, distancing and keeping himself far from it.

87:10.essay_html:
Verse 10 says the reminder will land on "whoever fears" 1,2,4,5,6,8,9,11,12,13,14. The commentators explain this as the person whose heart fears Allah, dreads His punishment, hopes for His reward, and knows he will meet Him. Because he expects to answer for his deeds, he holds back from wrongdoing and reaches for what is good 4,5.

al-Qurtubi (d. 1273) relays a report that this verse came down concerning Ibn Umm Maktum, though he leaves it unassessed 3. He also passes on two explanations for why the verse names "the one who fears" rather than "the one who hopes." al-Mawardi held that admonition reaches the fearful more forcefully than it reaches the hopeful, even though both may in fact benefit from it 3. al-Qushayri is cited for another view: the Prophet's ﷺ reminding was meant for everyone, since even where it fails to move the unready hearer, the act of reminding still earns its speaker reward 3.

Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021) reads the verse against the world's own signs: a serviceable animal like the camel obedient to man, the sky, the earth serving human need without effort on our part. These, he says, remind the thoughtful of God and the Hereafter. Whoever draws remembrance from them has earned a claim on God's lasting bounty; whoever stays lost in heedlessness has shown he deserves to be deprived of it, forever 10.

Verse 11 turns to the opposite case. "The most wretched" (al-ashqa) avoids the reminder, keeping his distance from it 1,2,3,5,9,11,12,13,14. al-Baghawi (d. 1122) and al-Qurtubi explain al-ashqa as the one already wretched in Allah's foreknowledge 2,3. Some said the verse was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah 3. al-Tabari (d. 923) transmits a saying of Qatadah: no servant turns from this reminder out of distaste and hatred for those who carry it, except one who is plainly, thoroughly wretched 1 (ungraded). al-Tantawi (d. 2010) notes the word may mean the whole class of the wretched, disbelievers in general, or a hardened individual such as Abu Jahl or al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah 9.

Sayyid Qutb (d. 1966) develops the picture further. The wretched one is wretched because his soul has fallen, because he fails to feel the truths held within the universe or read its signs, because he chases the petty gains of this world and wears himself out for them, and, in the Hereafter, because an endless Hellfire with no limit to its ages awaits him. Against this he sets the deliverance, success and purification open to the one who heeds 6.

Verse 12 names his destination: "the Greatest Fire" (al-nar al-kubra) 1,2,5,9,11,12,13,14. al-Tabari and al-Baghawi say it is called "greatest" for the intensity of its heat and pain, far exceeding any fire known in this world 1,2. al-Qurtubi records two further readings: al-Farra' held that "the Greatest" names the lowest of Hell's layers 3, while al-Hasan and Yahya ibn Sallam took it as the Fire of the Hereafter itself, set against "the lesser" fire of this world 3. Sayyid Qutb reads "greatest" as pointing to the Fire's overwhelming severity, its endless duration, and the vastness of a stay that never ends 6.

Verse 13 closes with the hardest line: he will "neither die therein nor live." Most of the commentators take this as meaning he will not die to find rest from the torment, nor will he live a life that does him any good 1,2,3,5,9,13. Ibn Kathir (d. 1373) adds that his continuing "life" actually works against him, since it is only the means by which he keeps on feeling the pain of the punishment 4. al-Tabari records a more physical explanation too: the soul of such a person lodges in his throat, neither leaving him (so that he might die) nor returning to its place in the body (so that he might live) 1. He also notes that Arabs used to describe a man in extreme hardship as "neither alive nor dead," and that the verse speaks to people in the very idiom they themselves used 1. al-Qurtubi cites a line of poetry carrying the same sense, of a soul that neither dies to end its suffering nor lives a life with any savour 3. al-Sa'di (d. 1957) ties the verse to a punishment without any rest or respite, so complete that its victims will wish for death and not find it, comparable to the Qur'an's description elsewhere that no reprieve is given them and nothing of the torment is eased 5.

Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr Zakariyya, and Ahsanul Bayaan all bring a hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (رضي الله عنه), recorded by Ahmad and in Sahih Muslim, that draws a further distinction. The permanent people of the Fire, it says, truly neither die nor live in it. But some, whom Allah intends for mercy, He causes to die in the Fire for their sins, until they turn to charcoal; then intercession is permitted, and they are brought out in groups and cast into a river of Paradise, sprouting again as a seed sprouts on the silt a flood leaves behind 4,11,12 (sahih, per Muslim). On this basis, Abu Bakr Zakariyya and Ahsanul Bayaan read "neither dying nor living" here as describing the utterly wretched disbeliever alone; the sinning believer's case in the Fire differs, since he eventually dies there and is later brought out through intercession 11,12. Israr Ahmad (d. 2010) links the whole phrase to the description of Hell in Surat al-Muddaththir, "it lets nothing remain and leaves nothing untouched," as another expression of the same total grip 8.

Between the fearful and the wretched of these verses lies one difference: whether the heart holds any fear of Allah at all. The one who fears is spoken for, and takes heed; the one without it turns away, and is left, as the commentators read it, in a fire and a state that is called neither life nor death 1,5,6.

87:19.title: Scriptures of Abraham and Moses
87:19.in_short: The surah ends by saying its message already stood in the earlier scriptures given to Abraham and Moses. The commentators discuss exactly what is being pointed to, what little is known of those lost scriptures' contents, and what this closing note teaches about the single source of true religion.

claims.text: Suhuf is the plural of sahifa (a leaf or page of writing); here it means the revealed books given to Abraham and Moses.

sources.original_excerpt: الصحف: فإنها جمع صحيفة، وإنما عُنِي بها: كتب إبراهيم وموسى

ইব্রাহীম ও মূসার গ্রন্থসমূহে

sources.original_excerpt: في الصحف التي أنـزلها الله إبراهيم وموسى أن الآخرة خير من الأولى

claims.text: Al-Ṭabarī preferred that 'this' refers back to the fuller preceding passage: success through purification, remembering God's name, praying, and preferring this life though the Hereafter is better and more lasting. Ibn Kathīr called this view good and strong, and noted it matches reports from Qatādah and Ibn Zayd.

sources.original_excerpt: لأن هذا إشارة إلى حاضر، فلأن يكون إشارة إلى ما قرب منها أولى
This view that he (At-Tabari) has chosen is good and strong.

claims.text: A broader reading holds that the whole surah, or at least its final major theme (the Hereafter being better and more lasting), was written in the earlier scriptures of Abraham and Moses; this is attributed to ʿIkrimah, al-Suddī, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah.

Abu `Aliyah said, "The story of this Surah is in the earlier Scriptures."

sources.original_excerpt: ولم يرد أن هذه الألفاظ بعينها في تلك الصحف، وإنما هو على المعنى

claims.text: In the same report, Abū Dharr then asked whether anything from those earlier scriptures had reached the Prophet ﷺ; the Prophet ﷺ answered yes, and told him to recite this very passage of the surah.

claims.text: A report from Qatādah via Abū al-Khuld states that the Scriptures of Abraham were sent down on the first night of Ramadan, the Torah on the sixth night, the Psalms (Zabūr) on the twelfth, the Gospel (Injīl) on the eighteenth, and the Qurʾān (al-Furqān) on the twenty-fourth.

claims.text: Al-Saʿdī notes that Abraham and Moses are the most honoured of the messengers besides the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and that the commands named in this surah recur in every revealed law, because they serve the welfare of both this world and the next, in every time and place.

sources.original_excerpt: اللذين هما أشرف المرسلين، سوى النبي محمد صلى الله وسلم عليه وسلم

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb reads the closing verse as testimony that the surah's themes are foundational articles of belief also present in the books of Abraham and Moses, showing that all religions come from the one God and the one will; differences between religions lie only in the branches of law, which God adjusted to the needs of each era, while the root of every revealed law is one, coming from the same Rabb al-Aʿlā (Most High Lord) who created man, proportioned him, and decreed and guided all things.

Rebar's commentary notes that because these matters appear in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses, they are likewise mentioned in the books of other prophets, and this is reason for Muslims to give the surah's message due attention.

Isrār Aḥmad observes that the Scriptures of Moses survive today in some form, but no clear trace of the Scriptures of Abraham remains; he states, as his own repeated opinion, that the Hindu Upanishads are a corrupted form of Abraham's scriptures.

He reads this build-up as raising the honour and standing of these scriptures.

sources.original_excerpt: وفى إبهام هذه الصحف، ووصفها بالقدم، ثم بيان أنها لنبيين كريمين... تنويه بشأنها، وإعلاء من قدرها

claims.text: Ibn Kathīr links this closing verse to a parallel passage in Surat al-Najm (53:36-42), which similarly refers to the Scriptures of Moses and of Abraham 'who fulfilled', and lists shared themes: no one bears another's burden, man has only what he strives for, his effort will be shown, he will be repaid in full, and the return is to his Lord.

sources.original_excerpt: This Ayah is similar to Allah's statement in Surat An-Najm

87:19.essay_html:
The surah closes with two short words that carry a great deal of weight: the Scriptures (ṣuḥuf) of Abraham and Moses 1,3,7,9,13,12. Ṣuḥuf is simply the plural of ṣaḥīfa, a written page, and here it names the revealed books given to these two prophets 1,3.

Commentators differ on exactly what 'this' (in the previous verse) refers back to. Ibn Zayd took it narrowly, as pointing only to the statement that the Hereafter is better than this present life 1. Al-Ṭabarī preferred a fuller reading: 'this' covers the whole preceding passage, success through purification, remembrance, and prayer, set against the choice to prefer this life though the Hereafter is better and more lasting. Ibn Kathīr called this reading good and strong 1,4. A still broader view, traced to ʿIkrimah, al-Suddī, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah, holds that the whole surah, or at least its closing theme, was already present in the Scriptures of Abraham and Moses 2,4,7,11. Al-Qurṭubī adds a caution here: this does not mean the exact wording stood in those earlier books, only that their meaning did 3.

A report traced to Abū Dharr describes what those lost scriptures were said to contain. The Scriptures of Abraham were all parables: a tyrant king is told that kingship was given him to carry the cry of the oppressed to God, not to hoard wealth, and the wise are told to divide their day between worship, self-reckoning, and provision, and to guard their tongue and their travels. The Scriptures of Moses were all sayings of astonishment: astonishment at one who believes in death yet rejoices, at one who believes in decree yet grieves, at one who sees the world turn yet trusts it, and at one who believes in the Reckoning yet does nothing. Abū Dharr then asked whether any of this had reached the Prophet ﷺ, who answered yes, and told him to recite this very passage 3,7. This report is relayed without a stated grading in the sources given, so it should be held as an ungraded report rather than an established fact.

Al-Ṭabarī also carries a separate report, from Qatādah by way of Abū al-Khuld, giving dates for when each scripture came down: Abraham's on the first night of Ramadan, the Torah on the sixth, the Psalms on the twelfth, the Gospel on the eighteenth, and the Qurʾān on the twenty-fourth 1. This too is passed on without a stated grading.

Several commentators draw out the wider point of naming these two scriptures. Al-Saʿdī notes that Abraham and Moses are the most honoured of the messengers besides the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and that the commands named in the surah recur in every revealed law, because they serve the good of both worlds at every time and place 5. Sayyid Quṭb reads the verse as testimony that all religions come from the one God and the one will: the root of every law is one, coming from the same Rabb al-Aʿlā (Most High Lord) who created man and proportioned him, even though the branches of law differ across eras according to their needs 6. Rebar's commentary makes a related point: because this matter appears in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses, it is also found in the books of other prophets, which is reason enough for Muslims to take it seriously 14.

Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) observes that something of Moses' Scriptures survives today, while no clear trace of Abraham's Scriptures remains. He offers, as his own repeated opinion, that the Hindu Upanishads are a corrupted form of Abraham's lost scriptures 8. This is presented in the source as a personal view rather than an established finding.

Ṭanṭāwī points to how the verse is built rhetorically: the reference is first left unnamed ('this'), then called merely 'the former scriptures', and only at the end named as belonging to two noble, resolute messengers, Abraham and Moses. He reads this rising sequence as deliberately raising the honour of these scriptures 9. Ibn Kathīr, for his part, links the verse to a parallel closing in Surat al-Najm, which also names the Scriptures of Moses and of 'Abraham who fulfilled', and lists shared themes: no soul bears another's burden, a man has only what he has striven for, his effort will be shown, and he will be repaid in full before returning to his Lord 4.

The surah's last word is that its message is not new: purification, remembrance, prayer, and the choice between a fading world and a lasting Hereafter were already written for Abraham and for Moses, and now stand named again at the end of this surah.

87:1.title: Glorify Him: Creation, Decree, Guidance
87:1.in_short: The surah opens by commanding the Prophet ﷺ to glorify his Lord who is Most High, then names four of His works: He creates and shapes in due proportion, He decrees and guides, and He brings out green pasture only to turn it into blackened debris.

claims.text: The Prophet ﷺ, and companions such as Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAli, Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Musa and Ibn Masʿud, used to respond to this verse by saying 'Subhana Rabbi al-Aʿla' (Glory to my Lord, the Most High) when reciting or hearing it.

sources.original_excerpt: سبحان ربي الأعلى

report.graded_by: not specified by the sources beyond citing the narration chains

claims.text: It is commendable (mustahab) to say 'Subhana Rabbi al-Aʿla' after reciting this verse; this recommendation applies outside of formal prayer, on the practice of the Companions.

When ʿAli was asked in prayer whether he was adding to the Qur'an by saying 'Subhana Rabbi al-Aʿla', he clarified that this was not Qur'anic text but something he had been commanded to do and had simply done.

sources.original_excerpt: إنما أمرنا بشيء فقلته

report.graded_by: al-Qurṭubī cites the chain without grading it

claims.text: A report states that when this Surah was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ instructed the Companions to say this tasbih in their prostration (sujud), just as an earlier verse's tasbih had been placed in the bowing (rukuʿ).

sources.original_excerpt: اجعلوها في سجودكم

report.graded_by: cited from Aḥmad's narration without further grading given

claims.text: Commentators differ on the exact sense of 'glorify the name of your Lord': some take it as simply 'exalt your Lord, the Most High' (with 'name' as an intensifying addition, not a separate object); others take it literally as 'keep the name of your Lord pure' meaning do not apply His names to idols, the way pagans named idols after Him (al-Lat, al-Uzza); others read 'sabbih' as 'pray' (salli), citing Ibn ʿAbbas's gloss 'pray by the command of your Lord, the Most High'.

Al-Ṭabarī states his own preferred reading: that the intended meaning is 'keep the name of your Lord pure from being invoked over idols and false gods', judging this most likely because the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions, on reciting it, understood it as exalting and purifying God's name.

sources.original_excerpt: نـزه اسم ربك أن تدعو به الآلهة والأوثان

claims.text: Some scholars argue that the sound tasbih response ('Subhana Rabbi' rather than 'Subhana Ism Rabbi') shows that 'ism' (name) here stands for the Divine Being Himself rather than literally 'a name'; this is used by those who hold that the Name and the Named are one and the same.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ notes that some of God's names are reserved for Him alone; people commit a fault by casually shortening names like ʿAbd al-Raḥmān or ʿAbd al-Ghaffār to 'Raḥmān' or 'Ghaffār' for a person, without regard for keeping such names exclusive to God.

Sayyid Quṭb reads the opening as establishing two divine attributes, Lordship (rubūbiyyah, nurturing care) and Highness (al-Aʿlā), whose combined tone sets the surah's gentle, elevated atmosphere and frames the universe itself as both a place of worship and a display of the Maker's works.
Al-Saʿdī explains that this tasbih is a command to remember and mention God's beautiful names in a way fitting His majesty, invoking each name's great meaning.

'Who created, then proportioned' (khalaqa fa-sawwa): the commentators agree this means God brought things into being and gave every creation a well-formed, balanced, proportionate shape, with no defect or imbalance.

Specific glosses on what was 'proportioned' vary: al-Kalbi said every living creature was given proportionate limbs (hands, feet, eyes); al-Zajjaj said man was created upright, his stature made even; al-Dahhak applied it to Adam specifically; other sayings held it meant created in the fathers' loins and proportioned in the mothers' wombs, or bodies created and understanding then proportioned.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ distinguishes 'khalaqa' (to create) from ordinary 'making': true creation means bringing something from pure non-existence into existence without any pre-existing material, a power belonging to God alone; 'sawwa' then means giving that creation a symmetrical, well-ordered structure of limbs and organs.

Readers differ over the vowelling of 'qaddara' (with or without doubling of the dal); most reciters double it, while ʿAli, al-Sulami and al-Kisāʾī read it lightened, though the commentators note both readings carry the same meaning.
The main reading of 'then guided' (fa-hada), following Mujahid, is that God guided man to the paths of good and evil, happiness and misery, and guided cattle to their grazing grounds.

An alternative reading, held by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Sudi, Muqatil and al-Kalbi, takes 'guided' to mean God taught the male how to approach the female for mating, linking this to 'Our Lord is He who gave everything its form, then guided it' (20:50).

Other reported readings of 'guided': that God decreed provisions and guided creatures to earning their livelihood; that He placed benefits within things and guided man to how to draw them out; and al-Sudi's view that God decreed the duration of the foetus in the womb and then guided it to its exit.

Al-Ṭabarī states his own preference here too: the verse's wording is general, so the guidance should be understood to cover all these reported senses together, not restricted to one, until decisive evidence narrows it.

Ibn Kathīr links this verse to Mūsā's saying to Firʿawn, 'Our Lord is He who gave everything its form and nature, then guided it aright' (20:50), and to a hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim that God decreed the measures of all creation fifty thousand years before creating the heavens and the earth, when His Throne was upon water.

report.graded_by: cited by Ibn Kathīr as recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim

claims.text: Isrār Aḥmad reads the four verbs (created, proportioned, decreed, guided) as marking stages of creation: the first two concern a thing's physical form (like a building's structure, then its finishing), while decree (qadar) fixes a creature's capacity, potential and limits, and guidance (hidāyah) is the instinctive knowledge implanted in every creature to fulfil its role, supplemented in man's case by revelation and prophets.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ likewise treats the four words as four attributes: creation from nothing, proportioning of form, decreeing a specific purpose for every created thing (citing Rūmī's Persian verse that earth, wind, water and fire are all obedient servants of God), and guidance of each thing to perform its function, extending this to the observation that man's own capacity for science and technology is itself part of this divinely-given guidance.

Sayyid Quṭb draws out 'decreed, then guided' at length: every level of creation, from the atom to the galaxy, is fitted and directed to its function; he cites the naturalist Cressy Morrison's observations on bird migration, homing pigeons, bees and eels as evidence, in the natural world, of guidance built into creatures that could not have arisen without a Creator behind it.
'Al-marʿā' (the pasture) refers to vegetation and herbage that animals graze on, described as growing in various colours, yellow, red, white and green.

Lexically, 'ghuthāʾ' is the dried, withered plant matter swept along like debris on the surface of a flood, and 'aḥwā' describes it turning blackened, from a colour verging on black after having been deep green.

original_terms.gloss: dried plant debris carried on floodwater

claims.text: Al-Ṭabarī records a grammarians' alternative account, that 'aḥwā' by hyperbaton (taqdīm/taʾkhīr) actually describes the pasture itself while still growing, deep green verging on black, citing a verse of Dhū al-Rumma as evidence, before it was later turned into dry debris; al-Ṭabarī himself rejects this reading, holding that the verse's plain word order already gives a sound sense without needing such rearrangement.

sources.original_excerpt: وهذا القول وإن كان غير مدفوع... غير صواب عندي

claims.text: Al-Saʿdī notes that this cycle of vegetation recalls God's worldly blessings, feeding people and every animal, and is placed alongside the surah's mention of religious blessings.

Sayyid Quṭb reads the vegetation cycle (green then black debris) as a sign pointing to the same fate awaiting all worldly life: this present life ends and comes to nothing, while the Hereafter, mentioned later in the surah, endures.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ takes the withering of green pasture into blackened stubble as also directing attention to man's own end: a healthy, radiant body is a divine gift with a limited term, which will eventually come to an end.

Wahiduddin Khan reads the arrangement of creation, serviceable animals, sky and earth disposed for man's benefit, as designed to remind a reflective person of God and the Hereafter; those who take heed secure God's lasting bounty, while those who remain heedless prove themselves deserving of being deprived of it.

87:1.essay_html:
The surah opens with a command: glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High. The commentators read this in several ways. Some take it simply as 'exalt your Lord', with 'name' added for emphasis. Others take it literally, as keeping God's name pure from being given to idols, the way the pagans named their gods after His names.1,3,9,7 Some read the opening word as 'pray', following a gloss from Ibn ʿAbbas.1,2,3 A further point, resting on the wording of the tasbih response itself, is that 'name' here may stand for God's Being, since the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions said 'Glory to my Lord' rather than 'Glory to the name of my Lord'.2,3,7

The Prophet ﷺ and several Companions, among them Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAli, Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Musa and Ibn Masʿud, used to answer this verse by saying 'Subhana Rabbi al-Aʿla', Glory to my Lord, the Most High.1,2,3,4,7,11,12 Commentators record this as commendable outside of prayer,3,7 and a further report has the Prophet ﷺ instructing that this tasbih be said in prostration.3,4,9,7 When ʿAli رضي الله عنه was once asked, after saying it in prayer, whether he was adding to the Qur'an, he explained that it was not Qur'anic text, only something he had been commanded to do.3 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976) adds that some of God's names belong to Him alone, and warns against the common habit of shortening names like ʿAbd al-Raḥmān to 'Raḥmān' for a person, careless of what is due to God's own names.7

Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads the opening as setting two attributes over the whole surah, Lordship and Highness, giving its gentle tone and lifting the whole universe into view as both a place of worship and a display of the Maker's craft.6 Al-Saʿdī (d. 1957) reads the tasbih as remembering God's beautiful names in a manner fitting His majesty.5

The Lord described is 'the One who created, then proportioned' (khalaqa fa-sawwā). The commentators agree that this means He brought things into being and gave every creation a balanced, well-formed shape, with nothing left unequal or amiss.1,2,3,4,5,7,9,11,13 Specific glosses vary: some apply it to every living creature's limbs, some to man's upright stature, some to Adam himself, some to the stages from conception to understanding.2,3 Muftī Shafīʿ distinguishes true creation, bringing something from pure non-existence, a power belonging to God alone, from ordinary making, which always uses existing material.7

The Lord is next 'the One who decreed, then guided' (qaddara fa-hadā). Readers differ on a small vowelling of 'decreed', though the sense is agreed to be the same either way.1,2,3 On what 'guided' means, Mujahid's reading, that God guided man to the paths of good and evil and guided cattle to their pastures, is widely relayed.1,2,3,4,11 Others read it as guiding the male to the female for mating, tying this to the same phrase in Sūrat Ṭāhā (20:50); others as guiding creatures to their livelihood, or the unborn to its time of birth.1,2,3 Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923), weighing these, judges that the wording is general and should be taken to cover all of them together, rather than being narrowed to one.1 Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) links the verse to the hadith that God decreed the measures of all creation fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth.4

Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) and Muftī Shafīʿ both draw out a fourfold structure across these two verses: creation and proportioning shape a thing's outward form, while decree fixes its capacity and limits, and guidance is the instinct built into it to carry out its purpose, in man's case completed by revelation.8,7 Sayyid Quṭb extends this into the natural world at length, citing the naturalist Cressy Morrison's observations on the homing instincts of birds, bees and eels as instances, visible to any observer, of a guidance built into creatures that points beyond themselves.6

The last of the four works named is that He 'brought out the pasture' (al-marʿā), the grasses and plants, in every colour, that feed the grazing animals.1,2,3,9,11,12 Then He 'made it dark debris' (ghuthāʾ aḥwā), dried stubble like the refuse a flood carries on its surface, its green having turned to black.1,2,3,4,9,11,12 Al-Ṭabarī notes a grammarians' alternative, that 'blackened' properly describes the pasture's deep green while still growing, quoting a line of Dhū al-Rumma in support, but sets this aside, holding that the verse's plain order already carries a sound meaning without need of rearrangement.1

Several commentators draw a lesson from this last image. Al-Saʿdī reads it as recalling God's worldly bounty in feeding creation, alongside the surah's religious bounty.5 Sayyid Quṭb takes the green-turned-black cycle as a sign of the fate of all worldly life, ending in nothing, set against the Hereafter which endures, a theme the surah returns to later.6 Muftī Shafīʿ applies it to man's own body, radiant with health for a time, but on a limited term that will end.7 Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021) reads the whole arrangement, serviceable animals, sky, earth and pasture, as built to remind a reflective person of God and of what comes after.10

Four works are named, creating, shaping, decreeing and guiding, and a fifth image follows them, the pasture that greens and then turns to debris, so that the One being glorified is known, in the commentators' reading, through what He does before He is named in words.

87:6.title: Recitation, Ease, and the Reminder
87:6.in_short: Allah promises the Prophet ﷺ that he will not forget what he is taught of the Qur'an, that Allah knows all that is open and hidden, that He will ease him toward the easy way, and commands him to go on reminding people wherever reminding helps.

claims.text: Allah promises the Prophet ﷺ that He will teach him the Qur'an and he will not forget it — a great glad tiding given directly to him.

Before this verse, the Prophet ﷺ used to rush to repeat each phrase as Jibril عليه السلام recited it to him, fearing he would forget it. This verse relieved him of that anxiety, similar to the earlier reassurance in Sūrat al-Qiyāmah (75:16-19) telling him not to hasten his tongue with the revelation.

Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads this as lifting from the Prophet's ﷺ shoulders the burden of preserving and memorising the Qur'an himself. It is glad tiding for him and, after him, for his community, since the safekeeping of the Qur'an rests on Allah's guarantee rather than on human memory alone.

Al-Rāzī, as related by Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010), sees a double sign in these verses: the Prophet ﷺ was unlettered yet retained this long book without study, repetition, or writing; and the surah is among the earliest Meccan revelations, so the promise itself was a foretelling of something yet to come, which indeed came to pass.

Many read the exception 'except what Allah wills' as pointing to abrogated verses (naskh): what Allah caused the Prophet ﷺ to forget corresponds to what He removed, whether in ruling or in recitation, comparable to the principle stated at 2:106.

original_terms.gloss: abrogation — one revealed ruling or recitation superseding another

claims.text: A related reading takes 'forgetting' here to mean 'leaving off practice' rather than losing the wording — i.e. it points to abrogation of what one acts upon, distinct from abrogation of what is recited.

Others, following al-Farrā', read the exception as a common Arabic idiom used in promises and oaths — one that preserves the completeness of the speaker's will in form without any real exception being intended, as in 'abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure, except what your Lord wills' (11:108). On this reading, Allah did not in fact will the Prophet ﷺ to forget anything.

A report holds that the Prophet ﷺ once omitted a verse while reciting in prayer. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb رضي الله عنه, present at the time, thought it had been abrogated, but on being asked the Prophet ﷺ said he had simply forgotten it. This is taken by some as showing that a momentary lapse followed by recollection does not contradict the promise of this verse.

report.graded_by: as relayed by al-Qurṭubī, Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ, and Abū Bakr Zakariyyā, without an explicit grading given

claims.text: On the grammar of 'falā tansā', some hold the 'lā' is a prohibition rather than a plain negation, with the extra letter kept only to preserve the verse's end-rhyme. Al-Qurṭubī and Ṭanṭāwī note this but prefer reading it as negation, since an exception from a prohibition is usually understood as temporary and bounded, and the letter in question is fixed in every written copy and every recitation of the Qur'an.

'He knows what is open and what is hidden' is explained as Allah's total knowledge of every deed and word, whether shown or concealed — nothing escapes Him. Some link the phrase specifically to what the Prophet ﷺ recited aloud with Jibril and what he repeated silently to himself out of fear of forgetting.
Ibn 'Abbās رضي الله عنه is cited giving a specific gloss: 'what is hidden' means what is in one's heart and self; others connect the phrase to charity given openly or in secret.
Al-Saʿdī (d. 1957) reads Allah's knowledge of the open and the hidden as including His knowledge of what truly benefits His servants — which is why He legislates and decrees exactly as He wills.

Sayyid Quṭb reads the exception 'except what Allah wills' as an instance of a standing Qur'anic principle: Allah's will is unconditioned, bound by no promise, so that even a true promise to His Prophet ﷺ still stands within the wider scope of His free will.
'We will ease you to the easy way' is understood as Allah making good deeds easy for the Prophet ﷺ and granting him an easy, tolerant Sharia (Law), with no hardship or crookedness in it.

original_terms.gloss: the easy way — the path or manner of ease

claims.text: Specific glosses on 'the easy way' differ: Ibn 'Abbās and Muqātil take it as the deeds of the people of Paradise; Ibn Masʿūd takes it as Paradise itself; al-Ḍaḥḥāk takes it as the easy, tolerant monotheistic law (al-ḥanafiyyah al-samḥah); others connect it back to the previous verse, meaning ease in receiving and retaining the revelation.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976) observes that the verse says 'We will facilitate you to the easiest way' rather than simply 'We will make the Sharia easy for you'. He takes this wording to mean Allah disposed the Prophet's ﷺ very nature toward the Sharia, so that he became its living embodiment rather than merely its recipient.

Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) notes that the verb form of 'nuyassiruka' carries a sense of gradualness. On this reading, Allah eases the Prophet's ﷺ path step by step, toward success in the struggle to establish the faith in this world, and toward Paradise and its comforts in the next.

Sayyid Quṭb extends this ease to describe the Prophet's ﷺ temperament itself, which he likens to the effortless harmony of the whole universe's motion. He supports this with reports of the Prophet ﷺ always choosing the easier of two options, and being gentle in trade, dress, food, and sleep.
The basic command in this verse is for the Prophet ﷺ to remind and preach with the Qur'an, warning people of Allah's greatness and His punishment.

Commentators offer several readings of the apparent condition 'if reminding benefits'. Some take it as a rhetorical figure rather than a genuine condition — comparable to 'garments that protect you from heat' (16:81), which implies cold too though only heat is stated — meaning reminding is commanded whether or not it visibly benefits. Others take the particle 'in' to mean 'idh' (since) or 'qad' (indeed), removing any sense of a real condition. Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) instead reads it as a genuine restriction: remind those it can actually help, excluding those whose disbelief has already proved a settled, hopeless matter.

Two companion sayings are cited on who benefits from reminding: Ibn 'Abbās said the reminder 'benefits my allies, not my enemies'; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said it is a reminder for the believer and a proof against the disbeliever.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ explains the particle 'in' here as emphatic rather than conditional, comparable to saying 'if you are a man, you must do this' — the underlying point being that reminding is always beneficial in some measure and so should never be abandoned.

Al-Saʿdī draws out an implied meaning: if reminding would not benefit — if it would increase evil or reduce good — then it is not commanded, and indeed becomes something to avoid. On this reading people divide into those who benefit from reminders and those who do not.

An etiquette of teaching is drawn from this verse: knowledge should not be spent on those unfit to receive it. 'Alī رضي الله عنه is cited saying, 'Do not tell people something their minds cannot grasp, for it will become a trial for some of them,' and, 'Tell people only what they know — would you want Allah and His Messenger rejected?'

report.graded_by: an athar attributed to 'Alī, relayed by Ibn Kathīr and Abū Bakr Zakariyyā without a stated grading

claims.text: Isrār Aḥmad clarifies that this verse does not mean the Prophet ﷺ should only remind people when he sees an immediate, visible response — a point he says the following verses of the surah go on to clarify further.

87:6.essay_html:
Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ that He will teach him the Qur'an and that he will not forget it, a plain and personal glad tiding.1,2,3,4,5,7,9,11,12,13,14 Before this, he had been rushing to repeat each phrase as Jibrīl عليه السلام recited it, afraid the words would slip away from him. This verse, echoing the earlier reassurance in Sūrat al-Qiyāmah, freed him of that fear.1,2,3,7,8,12 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads this as lifting a heavy burden from the Prophet's ﷺ shoulders: the safekeeping of the Qur'an is now Allah's guarantee, not a task left to human memory, and this is glad tiding for the whole community that comes after him too.6 Al-Rāzī, as reported by Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010), finds a double sign here: an unlettered man retaining this whole book without study or writing, and a promise given in the earliest days of the message that plainly came true.9

The exception, 'except what Allah wills', is read several ways. Many take it as pointing to abrogated material (naskh) — verses whose ruling or recitation Allah later removed.1,2,3,4,7,11,13,14 Others read 'forgetting' here as 'leaving off practice', abrogation of what is acted upon rather than of the words themselves.1,3 A third reading, following al-Farrā', treats the whole exception as an Arabic idiom of completeness rather than a real exception — as in the phrase 'abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure, except what your Lord wills' — meaning Allah did not, in fact, will him to forget anything.1,3,9 A report adds that the Prophet ﷺ once left out a verse in prayer; Ubayy ibn Kaʿb رضي الله عنه thought it abrogated, but the Prophet ﷺ told him he had simply forgotten it — taken by some as showing that a passing lapse, quickly recalled, does not break the promise of this verse.3,7,11 A finer grammatical question is whether the 'lā' of 'falā tansā' forbids or merely denies; al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) and Ṭanṭāwī prefer denial, since the letter is fixed in every copy of the Qur'an and every recitation.3,9 Sayyid Quṭb ties the exception to a wider Qur'anic principle: Allah's will is never bound, not even by His own true promise.6

'He knows what is open and what is hidden' is read as covering every deed and word, shown or concealed, some linking it to what the Prophet ﷺ recited aloud and what he murmured to himself in fear of forgetting.1,2,3,4,5,9,12,13,14 Ibn 'Abbās رضي الله عنه glossed 'hidden' as what is in the heart; others tied it to charity given openly or secretly.3 Al-Saʿdī takes it further: this knowledge includes what truly benefits Allah's servants, which is why He legislates and decrees exactly as He wills.5

'We will ease you to the easy way' is taken as Allah making good deeds easy for the Prophet ﷺ and giving him a tolerant Sharia with no hardship in it.1,2,3,4,5,9,11,12,13,14 Exactly what 'the easy way' (al-yusrā) means is put differently by different voices: the deeds of the people of Paradise, Paradise itself, the easy monotheistic law, or simply ease in receiving the revelation.2,3 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976) notes the Qur'an says 'facilitate you to the easy way' rather than 'make the law easy for you' — as if Allah shaped the Prophet's ﷺ very nature to the Sharia, so he became its living embodiment.7 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) reads the verb form as carrying gradualness: ease coming to the Prophet ﷺ step by step, in this world's struggle and in the next world's reward.8 Sayyid Quṭb carries the theme into the Prophet's ﷺ character itself, likening it to the effortless harmony of the universe's motion, and pointing to reports of him always taking the easier of two choices, gentle in trade, food, dress, and sleep.6

'So remind, if reminding will help' commands the Prophet ﷺ to keep preaching and warning.1,2,3,4,5,7,9,11,12,13,14 The word 'if' has drawn several readings. Some take it as a figure of speech, not a real condition — like saying garments protect 'from heat' when cold is meant too — so reminding is due regardless of visible benefit.2,3,9 Others read 'if' as meaning 'since' or 'indeed'.3 Al-Ṭabarī (d. 923), by contrast, reads it as a real restriction: remind those it can actually help, setting aside those whose rejection has already proved final.1 Ibn 'Abbās said the reminder 'benefits my allies, not my enemies'; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī called it a reminder for the believer and a proof against the disbeliever.3 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ reads 'if' as emphatic rather than conditional — like 'if you are a man, you must do this' — meaning reminding is always worthwhile and should never be dropped.7 Al-Saʿdī draws the opposite implication: where reminding would only increase evil or shrink good, it is not commanded at all, so people fall into those who benefit from a reminder and those who do not.5 From the verse, 'Alī رضي الله عنه's counsel is cited as an etiquette of teaching: do not burden people with what their minds cannot hold, and tell them only what they can bear.4,11 Isrār Aḥmad adds that this is not a licence to preach only where a response is already visible, a point the following verses go on to settle.8

The passage moves from a private assurance to the Prophet ﷺ that his memory of the revelation is secured, through the ease Allah grants him in carrying it, to a plain charge: keep reminding, wherever the reminder can do good.
